get_27_day_outlook.description: Read SWPC's four-week outlook: for each of the next 27 days, the expected solar radio flux, the planetary A index and the highest K index, with the storm level each one implies. Issued once a week and covering one solar rotation - how long it takes an active region to come back around - so it is a tendency rather than a forecast for a date, and it is the right thing to read when planning weeks ahead.

get_aurora_forecast.description: Answer whether the aurora is likely to be visible from one place in the next hour. Give a latitude and longitude and you get the percentage chance of aurora directly overhead, and - when there is none overhead - how far away the nearest aurora is and which way to look. Works in both hemispheres, and comes with the power flowing into the aurora as a whole, which is the number that says whether tonight is ordinary or exceptional.

get_current_conditions.description: Read what space weather is doing right now: whether a geomagnetic storm, a radio blackout or a radiation storm is in progress and how bad, the planetary K index, how fast the solar wind is blowing and which way its magnetic field points, and the Sun's radio output. Each storm comes back on NOAA's own 1-to-5 scale with the word that goes with it, and a one-line summary a workflow can send as it stands.

Each day carries a one-line summary.

get_forecast_discussion.description: Read the write-up SWPC's forecasters publish three times a day explaining what the Sun has done in the last 24 hours and what they expect next - the reasoning behind the numbers, naming the regions, the coronal holes and the coronal mass ejections involved. It comes back split into its four sections (solar activity, energetic particles, solar wind and geospace), each with its summary and its forecast, plus the original text.

Each reading carries its NOAA storm level, so a step can act on 'G2' rather than working out what 6.33 means. Defaults to the last 24 hours; about a week is published.

get_solar_wind.description: Read the solar wind arriving at Earth: how fast it is blowing, how dense it is, how hot it is, and which way its magnetic field points. The north-south component is the one that matters - when it turns southward the solar wind couples to the Earth's field and a storm can start - so the answer says so in words as well as numbers. Measured a million miles upstream, so it is an hour of warning.

list_alerts.description: List the watches, warnings, alerts and summaries SWPC has issued - the notices that go out to power grid operators, airlines and satellite teams. Each one comes back as fields rather than a block of teleprinter text: what it is about, how urgent it is, when it starts and ends, its NOAA scale and its potential impacts. Filter by kind and by subject. About the last 30 days are published, and a quiet spell returns nothing rather than failing.

list_solar_flares.description: List the solar flares SWPC has recorded, with when each one started, peaked and ended, its class, the sunspot region it came from, and the radio blackout it caused on NOAA's scale. Two GOES satellites watch the Sun and report the same flare twice, so each flare appears once here, at the larger of the two readings. Defaults to C-class and above over the last week; about 30 days are published.

Defaults to the most recent day. Choose a region instead and you get every day it has been reported, so you can watch it grow or decay as it crosses the disk.

description: Read space weather from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center, the official US source: whether a geomagnetic storm, radio blackout or radiation storm is in progress, the three-day forecast and the four-week outlook, the alerts that go out to power grids and airlines, the solar wind arriving at Earth, the flares and sunspot regions on the Sun, and the forecasters' own write-up. Also answers the question most people come for: whether the aurora will be visible tonight from a given latitude and longitude. Every storm comes back on NOAA's plain 1-to-5 scale. No account or API key required.
